guide.title: Mohawk Mountain: A 1947 Lease, a Snowmaking Dispute, and the Path to Mount Snow, Butternut, and Sundown
guide.intro: Mohawk Mountain traces to a lease Walt Schoenknecht signed with the State of Connecticut in February 1947 for about 100 acres on the northwest side of the mountain, on a peak known as the Pinnacle, per New England Ski History. The new area "reportedly debuted the day after Christmas in 1947," per that source's own hedge, opening for the 1947-48 season. Mohawk Mountain's own history page, in a passage originally rendered in all capitals, states: "in 1947 Walt Schoenknecht opened Mohawk Mountain Ski Area for all to enjoy," and that the mid-mountain Pine Lodge "was the Schoenknecht family home for many years before Mohawk Mountain Ski Area opened in 1947." Schoenknecht went on to found a second area: while still running Mohawk, he purchased land on Mt. Pisgah in southern Vermont around May 1953, telling the Hartford Courant, per New England Ski History, "The mountain has fantastic possibilities," and following the 1953-54 season he announced the formation of the Mount Snow Development Corp; Mount Snow opened for the winter of 1954-55. Mohawk's own page states plainly: "Walt also founded Mount Snow." Schoenknecht was inducted into the National Ski Hall of Fame — today the U.S. Ski & Snowboard Hall of Fame — as a Class of 1979 inductee in the Resort category, per that organization's own inductee page, which lists him as born in 1919 in East Haven, Connecticut, and died in 1987, consistent with New England Ski History's account that he passed away prior to the start of the 1987-88 season at age 68.

sections.heading: Two accounts of who pioneered snowmaking
sections.body: Mohawk's own history page states that "Walt was the pioneer of manmade snowmaking, leading the efforts behind the technology that is used worldwide today" — the operator's own framing of Schoenknecht's role. New England Ski History gives a more granular, and different, account: in the winter of 1949-50, after a snow drought, Schoenknecht purchased an estimated 500 tons of ice from Economy Ice Company and used a chipper to create a snow surface, allowing Mohawk to reopen its Pinnacle Trail and Pine Slope on January 22, 1950 — a manual ice-chipping method distinct from mechanical snowmaking. Separately, on March 15, 1950, Arthur Hunt of Tey Company announced the invention of snow-making machines that could be positioned "at intervals along a trail" using "a pressurized system," explicitly distinguishing his invention from Mohawk's chopped-ice system by stating that, to his knowledge, his company was the first to convert water to snow in an open field. For the 1950-51 season, per New England Ski History, "Mohawk and Split Rock (later known as Big Boulder, PA) boasted the first two snowmaking systems using equipment invented by Tey Manufacturing's Wayne M. Pierce Jr." The system was first tested the night of December 28, 1950, an attempt that "ended inconclusively when below zero cold froze feed lines of the device after only a small amount of snow was produced"; two days later Mohawk announced three snow-making machines had been in operation. Both accounts are published here as each source states them: the resort's own page credits Schoenknecht as snowmaking's pioneer, while New England Ski History's more granular account credits the actual 1950-51 machinery to Tey Manufacturing's Wayne Pierce, with Schoenknecht's own 1949-50 contribution being the manual ice-chipping workaround rather than the machine itself. Mohawk's own history page separately states the ski area "offers 112 skiable acres over 300 scenic acres of state forest" — an operator-stated figure, attributed here to the operator's own page rather than restated as settled fact.

sections.heading: Channing Murdock: Mohawk to Butternut Basin to Ski Sundown
sections.body: Schoenknecht ordered Carlevaro & Savio chairlifts for the 1960-61 season, including one for Mohawk Mountain, which New England Ski History describes as "the first chairlift installed in southern New England"; Channing Murdock "was hired to manage the upgraded area." Following the 1961-62 season, per that same source, "Channing Murdock departed to start Butternut Basin. A few years later, he acquired the defunct Satan's Ridge ski area, reopening it as Ski Sundown" — tying Murdock's Mohawk tenure to both Butternut Basin, in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, and, later, Ski Sundown in New Hartford, Connecticut. The Berkshire Edge, in a January 8, 2024 article on Ski Butternut's 60th anniversary, independently corroborates the Mohawk connection: "In 1962, Channing Murdock, a former employee of Mount Snow in Vt., and former manager of Mohawk Mountain in Cornwall, Conn., purchased the property with his wife, Jane Murdock," referring to the Warner Mountain property the couple reopened as Butternut Basin, now Ski Butternut, on Christmas Eve 1963.

sections.heading: The 1989 tornado, night skiing, and family continuity
sections.body: An F4 tornado struck Mohawk Mountain at 4:37 p.m. on July 10, 1989, causing $1.5 to $2 million in damage, destroying buildings and toppling lifts, per New England Ski History; initial industry analysis held the ski area might not reopen for a year, if ever, but Mohawk rebuilt in time to open for the 1989-90 season. Mohawk's own history page corroborates the event in general terms: "in 1989, a tornado hit Mohawk Mountain, destroying much of the surrounding forest and damaging the lifts and structures." The same 1989 tornado outbreak also destroyed most of nearby Cathedral Pines, a Nature Conservancy preserve elsewhere in Cornwall (see below). In the fall of 1991, the State of Connecticut agreed to allow night skiing at Mohawk under a fifteen-point list of requirements, added that winter in part to help pay off tornado-related debt, with alcohol remaining banned on the state property. Schoenknecht signed a new 30-year lease with the State of Connecticut starting January 1986, providing up to 1.85% of gross revenue to the state; a further 30-year lease began in January 2017, per the same source. Mohawk's own page states Walt opened the mountain "the same year his daughter, Carol Lugar, was born," and that "today, Mohawk Mountain is still family owned and operated with Carol as co-owner and president"; New England Ski History separately notes that Walt was diagnosed with cancer in the early 1980s and that Carol Lugar returned to help him manage the area.

faq.question: Who founded Mohawk Mountain, and what else did he found?
faq.answer: Walt Schoenknecht, per a February 1947 lease with the State of Connecticut and Mohawk's own history page ("Walt also founded Mount Snow"). Mount Snow opened for the 1954-55 season after Schoenknecht bought land on Mt. Pisgah, Vermont, around 1953. He was inducted into the National Ski Hall of Fame as a Class of 1979 inductee.

faq.question: Did Walt Schoenknecht invent snowmaking?
faq.answer: Mohawk's own history page calls him "the pioneer of manmade snowmaking," but New England Ski History's more granular account credits the actual 1950-51 machinery to Tey Manufacturing's Wayne Pierce, describing Schoenknecht's own 1949-50 role as manual ice-chipping rather than a machine. Both accounts are published here, attributed, without resolving the disagreement.

faq.question: What happened during the 1989 tornado?
faq.answer: An F4 tornado struck Mohawk at 4:37 p.m. on July 10, 1989, causing $1.5 to $2 million in damage and toppling lifts, per New England Ski History; Mohawk rebuilt in time for the 1989-90 season. The same tornado outbreak also destroyed most of nearby Cathedral Pines, a Nature Conservancy preserve in Cornwall.

faq.question: Where else can I go in Cornwall?
faq.answer: This guide covers only Mohawk Mountain itself. Cornwall's other places — the West Cornwall Covered Bridge, Mohawk State Forest, Housatonic Meadows State Park, Cornwall Market, and the Cornwall Inn among them — are on the town's own travel guide, linked below.

places.name: Cathedral Pines
places.address: Essex Hill Road, Cornwall, CT 06753 (parking at the foot of Essex Hill, per the Town of Cornwall's own website)
places.summary: A 42-acre old-growth white pine and hemlock preserve in Cornwall, owned and managed by The Nature Conservancy and open to the public, devastated by the same 1989 tornado outbreak that hit Mohawk Mountain.
places.history: Cathedral Pines is a 42-acre old-growth forest preserve in Cornwall, Connecticut, owned and managed by The Nature Conservancy and open to the public, per Wikipedia's article on the preserve. Wikipedia states the preserve "was mostly destroyed by tornadoes in July 1989" — the same tornado outbreak that struck Mohawk Mountain elsewhere in Cornwall. The Nature Conservancy's own preserve page corroborates the event, describing what had been "New England's largest stand of old-growth white pine and hemlock trees" as "devastated by three tornadoes in July 1989," and states that a trail today "traverses the remaining intact portion of the stand." The Town of Cornwall's own website directs visitors to "meet at Cathedral Pines Parking at the foot of Essex Hill."
